patient.name: Joanne Whitfield
patient.complaint: Constant worry, poor sleep and a racing heart for 8 months
background: Divorced last year; lone parent of two children in Walthamstow
Office manager; recently missing days at work
No regular medicines; drinks 2 glasses of wine most evenings

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with months of worry about many things, physical anxiety symptoms and normal tests. Distractors: panic disorder, depression, hyperthyroidism.

points: Joanne, 44: 'I can't switch my brain off.'
Worries about work, money, the children and her health.
Tired, irritable, tense shoulders, wakes at 3 am.

steps.lead: Joanne's worry is excessive, hard to control and spread across **many** areas of life, not one specific fear.
Joanne is **44**, recently divorced, a lone parent, with a family history: several risk factors at once.

visual.title: How long has the worry lasted?
visual.label: Joanne 8 months
visual.caption: At least 6 months of excessive worry is needed for GAD.

points: Fine tremor of the hands; palms sweaty.
Answers take long detours before reaching the point (**circumstantiality**).
Mood 'fed up' but enjoys her children; no suicidal thoughts.

steps.lead: Joanne has the core worry for over 6 months plus restlessness, irritability, tension, poor sleep and somatic symptoms.

steps.q: Joanne also has palpitations and a tremor. Which mimic must you exclude first?
steps.r: **Hyperthyroidism** causes tremor, sweating, palpitations and anxiety; check TFTs before labelling GAD.

steps.lead: Joanne has no sudden attacks of terror, so this is not panic disorder. Her **thyroid** still needs checking.

steps.title: GAD vs panic disorder
head: Feature
GAD
Panic disorder
rows: Fear of dying or losing control

steps.lead: Joanne's evening wine and low mood show how GAD drifts into **substance misuse** and **depression**.

steps.text: Do not jump to depression because she is tired and sleeps badly. Ask whether **worry** or **low mood and loss of interest** is the core feature.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (TFTs or baseline bloods to exclude a mimic). GAD itself is a clinical diagnosis; Holter only when palpitations have worrying features.

steps.q: What confirms that Joanne has GAD?
steps.r: GAD is diagnosed by **clinical assessment**. Tests only exclude mimics.

steps.lead: Joanne's history and mental state exam make the diagnosis. No blood test proves GAD.

steps.title: Joanne's baseline bloods
steps.text: All normal: no anaemia, thyrotoxicosis or diabetes to explain her symptoms.

steps.lead: Joanne's FBC, TFTs, glucose and U&Es are normal, so an organic cause is unlikely.

visual.title: Joanne's TSH
visual.label: Joanne 1.9
visual.caption: A normal TSH rules out hyperthyroidism as the cause of her tremor and palpitations.

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: Sinus rhythm, 92 bpm, no other abnormality.

steps.text: Joanne's ECG is normal, as it typically is in GAD.

steps.lead: Joanne's palpitations happen when she is worrying at rest. If they came on **exercise** or with **near-syncope**, a Holter would be needed.

steps.text: In the exam, 'Which investigation?' for an anxious patient with palpitations and tremor is usually **TFTs**.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' (education and CBT) and next steps: sertraline, then another SSRI or an SNRI. Know review timing and why benzodiazepines are avoided.

steps.q: Joanne wants help but is wary of tablets. What is the most important first-line treatment?
steps.r: **CBT** is the most important first-line treatment, after education and low-intensity self-help.

steps.lead: Joanne starts with **education**, a self-help CBT workbook and a psychoeducation group, with CBT as the key treatment.

steps.title: Stepped care for GAD
steps.caption: Step up only if the previous step has not worked.

points: Three months later: still not coping, now off work.
She agrees to **sertraline** alongside high-intensity CBT.
Warned it takes **2 to 4 weeks** and may worsen anxiety at first.
Review every 2 to 4 weeks for 3 months (she is over 30).

steps.lead: Joanne has stepped up to sertraline. Beta-blockers could ease her racing heart; benzodiazepines are avoided long-term.

visual.title: Joanne's GAD-7 score on sertraline
visual.caption: Slightly worse in week 1, then steady improvement from 2 to 4 weeks.

steps.text: A patient **under 30** starting an SSRI is reviewed at **1 week**, not 2 to 4 weeks.

steps.lead: Joanne has no suicidal thoughts. If she did, or stopped coping with daily life, she would need **urgent mental health review**.
NICE CG113 sets out the stepped-care pathway used for Joanne.

steps.text: If sertraline fails or is not tolerated: **another SSRI** or an **SNRI** (venlafaxine, duloxetine), not a benzodiazepine.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why panic attacks cause tingling, why SSRIs take weeks and can worsen anxiety at first, and why benzodiazepines cause dependence.

steps.lead: Joanne's tremor, sweating and racing heart come from **chronic sympathetic activation** driven by an overactive threat system.

steps.title: If Joanne had a panic attack: blood gas
steps.text: Acute respiratory alkalosis with a low ionised calcium: hyperventilation.

steps.lead: Hyperventilation blows off CO2. Alkalosis makes albumin bind more calcium, so **free calcium falls** and the lips and fingers tingle.
This is why Joanne felt worse in week 1 and better by week 4: serotonin rises fast, but limbic changes take weeks.

steps.q: Joanne asks for diazepam 'to keep me going'. Why is long-term use avoided?
o: GABA-A receptor downregulation causes tolerance and dependence
It blocks serotonin reuptake too strongly
steps.r: Long-term benzodiazepines **downregulate GABA-A receptors**: tolerance, dependence and rebound anxiety on stopping.

steps.lead: Propranolol would calm Joanne's racing heart, but would not touch her **worry**. Diazepam would work short-term at the cost of dependence.

mcq.q: What is the minimum duration of excessive worry for a diagnosis of GAD?
mcq.r: **At least 6 months** of excessive, uncontrollable worry.

mcq.q: Which condition is the most important mimic of GAD to exclude?
mcq.r: **Hyperthyroidism** causes tremor, sweating, palpitations and anxiety.

mcq.q: Which age band carries the highest risk of GAD in the notes?
mcq.r: Age **35–54** is a listed risk factor, along with divorce, living alone and lone parenthood.

mcq.q: What causes paraesthesia during a panic attack?
o: Low ionised calcium from respiratory alkalosis
mcq.r: Hyperventilation causes **respiratory alkalosis**, lowering ionised calcium.
GAD is a **clinical** diagnosis; bloods exclude mimics.

mcq.q: When should a Holter monitor be considered in an anxious patient?
o: New palpitations on exercise or with near-syncope

mcq.q: What is the most important first-line treatment for GAD?
Which is the first-line drug for severe GAD?
mcq.r: **Sertraline** (SSRI); venlafaxine or another SSRI if it fails.

mcq.q: When is a 24 year old reviewed after starting an SSRI?
Why is long-term benzodiazepine use avoided?
mcq.r: **GABA-A downregulation** causes tolerance, dependence and rebound anxiety.

technique.stem: A 47 year old man has a 9 month history of worrying about his job, his finances and his elderly parents. He finds he cannot stop the worry, sleeps badly and has tense shoulders. He feels restless and irritable. He has no sudden episodes of intense fear. His pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 132/82 mmHg. Thyroid function is normal.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about chronic worry: decide pattern, duration and focus.

clues: his job, his finances and his elderly parents
no sudden episodes of intense fear
steps.x: Over 6 months, many domains, uncontrollable, no discrete attacks, mimic excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Generalised anxiety disorder.**

elim: Adjustment disorder follows a clear stressor and is shorter-lived.
Depression needs low mood or loss of interest as the core feature.
Thyroid function is normal.
Panic disorder needs recurrent sudden attacks; he has none.

steps.x: **C. GAD.** Rule: 6 months + many worries + no attacks + normal TFTs = GAD.

technique.stem: A 38 year old woman has a 7 month history of constant worry, poor sleep, sweating and a fine tremor. She has lost 1 kg. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg. She has no neck swelling. Her GP suspects generalised anxiety disorder.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

steps.x: Initial investigation: what must be excluded before calling this GAD?
Tremor, sweating, tachycardia and slight weight loss overlap with thyrotoxicosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Thyroid function tests** (with baseline FBC, glucose, U&Es).

elim: Holter is for palpitations on exercise or with near-syncope.
No chest symptoms are described.
No neurological features.
Cortisol is not part of the GAD work-up.

steps.x: **E. TFTs.** Rule: always exclude hyperthyroidism in suspected GAD.

technique.stem: A 26 year old man with generalised anxiety disorder has not improved with a self-help programme and individual CBT. He has severe symptoms and is struggling at work. His GP starts sertraline.
technique.q: When is the most appropriate time for his first review?
o: Only if he contacts the surgery

steps.x: This is about SSRI follow-up timing; the age is the key fact.
He is under 30 and starting an SSRI.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Under 30: review at **1 week**.

elim: 3 months is far too late to check side effects and worsening anxiety.
2 to 4 weekly reviews are for patients over 30.
6 months is far too late.
Active follow-up is needed, not patient-initiated.

steps.x: **A. After 1 week.** Rule: SSRI under 30 = review at 1 week.

technique.stem: A 52 year old woman has taken diazepam every day for 3 years for generalised anxiety disorder. She now needs higher doses for the same effect, and when she misses a dose she becomes shaky and more anxious than before.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?

steps.x: Mechanism question: tolerance and withdrawal on a benzodiazepine.

clues: higher doses for the same effect
steps.x: Tolerance plus rebound anxiety on missing doses means dependence.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Chronic benzodiazepines cause **GABA-A receptor downregulation**.

elim: Serotonin reuptake relates to SSRIs, not diazepam.
MAO inhibition is the action of MAOIs.
Beta-blockade is how propranolol works.
Dopamine receptors are not the target of benzodiazepines.

steps.x: **A. GABA-A receptor downregulation.**

practice.stem: A 41 year old woman has a 10 month history of feeling on edge. She worries about her children, her mortgage and her health, and cannot control it. She has muscle tension, poor concentration and wakes at night. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. She still enjoys time with friends and denies low mood.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Excessive, uncontrollable worry about many areas for over 6 months with muscle tension and poor sleep is GAD. Depression needs low mood or anhedonia as the core.

steps.x: Diagnosis: chronic anxiety symptoms.

clues: her children, her mortgage and her health
steps.x: More than 6 months of uncontrollable worry about many areas, with somatic symptoms; mood preserved.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Generalised anxiety disorder.**

elim: She enjoys things and denies low mood.
OCD has obsessions and compulsions.
No sudden discrete attacks.
No trauma or flashbacks.

steps.x: **B. GAD.**

practice.stem: A 50 year old man has felt tense and worried about everything for a year. He has palpitations, sweating and a fine tremor. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 134/84 mmHg. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: Sinus rhythm, 92 bpm, no other abnormality.

practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Chronic generalised worry with somatic symptoms, a normal ECG and normal thyroid function is GAD. Normal TFTs exclude hyperthyroidism.

steps.x: Diagnosis with physical symptoms: are the tests normal?

clues: tense and worried about everything for a year
palpitations, sweating and a fine tremor
steps.x: Chronic worry plus somatic symptoms. The ECG is sinus rhythm and TFTs are normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **GAD**, with mimics excluded.

elim: The ECG shows sinus rhythm, not AF.
TSH and free T4 are normal.
Phaeochromocytoma causes paroxysmal attacks with severe hypertension.
SVT is a paroxysmal narrow-complex tachycardia; this is sinus.

steps.x: **B. GAD.** The ECG is typically normal in GAD.

practice.stem: A 36 year old woman says she has worried excessively about her family, work and health for 7 months. She feels restless, tired and irritable. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg. A mental state examination is performed.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on mental state examination?
practice.e: In GAD the mental state exam shows anxious affect, restlessness and tension. Circumstantial speech may also be seen.

steps.x: Most likely MSE finding in this presentation.

clues: worried excessively about her family, work and health for 7 months
steps.x: This is GAD; MSE shows anxiety, not psychosis, mania or depression.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Anxious affect with restlessness** and tension.

elim: Flight of ideas suggests mania.
Formal thought disorder suggests psychosis.
Psychomotor retardation suggests depression.
Thought insertion is a first-rank symptom of schizophrenia.

steps.x: **A. Anxious affect with restlessness.**

practice.stem: A GP reviews the records of five patients with persistent worry. She wants to know which one has the highest risk of generalised anxiety disorder, based on age and social circumstances.
practice.q: Which patient is at the highest risk?
o: A 19 year old student living with his parents
A 28 year old married man with no illness
A 45 year old divorced lone mother living alone with her son
A 70 year old married retired teacher
An 82 year old woman in a care home
practice.e: GAD risk factors include age 35 to 54, being divorced or separated, living alone and being a lone parent. This patient has all of them.

steps.x: Risk factor question: match each patient to the listed risk factors.
Risk factors: age 35 to 54, divorced or separated, living alone, lone parent.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The **45 year old divorced lone mother** has several at once.

elim: Young and living with family: fewer risk factors.
Married, outside the peak age, no illness.
Outside the peak age and married.
Outside the peak age.

steps.x: **C. The 45 year old divorced lone mother.**

practice.stem: A 39 year old man has had generalised anxiety disorder for 3 years and has not sought treatment. He now drinks a bottle of wine each night to 'calm his nerves'. His pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 138/86 mmHg. He has lost interest in his hobbies and feels hopeless.
practice.q: Which complication of generalised anxiety disorder has he most likely developed?
practice.e: GAD can lead to depression and substance misuse. Loss of interest and hopelessness show depression has developed.

steps.x: Complication of untreated GAD.
Anhedonia and hopelessness on top of long-standing GAD, plus alcohol misuse.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Depression**, a recognised complication of GAD.

elim: No episodes of elevated mood.
No cognitive decline described.
No obsessions or compulsions.
No psychotic features.

steps.x: **C. Depression.** Substance misuse is the other complication shown here.

practice.stem: A 33 year old woman with generalised anxiety disorder is brought to ED after a sudden episode of breathlessness, chest tightness and fear of dying. She has tingling around her mouth and in her fingers. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 136/84 mmHg and respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her tingling?
practice.e: Hyperventilation during a panic attack causes respiratory alkalosis, which lowers ionised calcium and causes perioral and peripheral paraesthesia.

steps.x: Cause of a symptom: what does hyperventilation do?

clues: tingling around her mouth and in her fingers
steps.x: A panic attack with hyperventilation causing respiratory alkalosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Alkalosis lowers **ionised calcium**, causing perioral and peripheral paraesthesia.

elim: No diabetes or drowsiness; glucose is not the mechanism.
Low potassium causes weakness and arrhythmias, not perioral tingling.
Hyperventilation causes alkalosis, not acidosis.
TIA gives focal deficits, not bilateral perioral tingling.

steps.x: **D. Reduced ionised calcium.**

practice.stem: A 45 year old man is thought to have generalised anxiety disorder after 8 months of constant worry, sweating and poor sleep. His pulse rate is 94 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg. Examination is otherwise normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: Baseline FBC, TFTs, glucose and U&Es exclude anaemia, hyperthyroidism and diabetes as contributors. The diagnosis itself is clinical.

steps.x: Initial investigation in suspected GAD.
Typical GAD; you need baseline tests to exclude mimics.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Baseline **FBC, TFTs, glucose and U&Es**.

elim: No neurological features.
No cardiac signs.
Cortisol is not part of the baseline work-up.
Nothing suggests drug misuse.

steps.x: **C. FBC, TFTs, glucose and U&Es.** Rules out anaemia, hyperthyroidism and diabetes.

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman with generalised anxiety disorder reports new episodes of palpitations while running, and once nearly fainted. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Her resting ECG is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
practice.e: New palpitations, particularly exercise-induced with near-syncope, warrant a 24 or 48-hour Holter. Do not attribute them to anxiety without excluding arrhythmia.

steps.x: Next investigation: are these palpitations anxiety or something else?

clues: new episodes of palpitations while running
steps.x: Exercise-induced palpitations with near-syncope are red flags, even with known GAD.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **24- or 48-hour Holter ECG.**

elim: No chest signs.
No features of PE.
Red-flag palpitations should not be blamed on anxiety.
Cortisol does not explain palpitations.

steps.x: **A. 24-hour Holter ECG.**

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman has a 6 month history of worry, fatigue, muscle tension and insomnia most days, interfering with her job. She has no depressive symptoms. She is reluctant to take medication but wants help. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: CBT is the most important first-line treatment for GAD. Sertraline is the first-line drug when symptoms are severe or psychological therapy has not worked.

steps.x: Management in a patient who prefers not to take medication.
GAD; she wants a non-drug option.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CBT**, the most important first-line treatment.

elim: Benzodiazepines are avoided long-term (dependence).
Pregabalin is not first-line.
Beta-blockers only treat somatic symptoms.
Sertraline is for severe GAD or if therapy fails; she declines tablets.

steps.x: **A. CBT.**

practice.stem: A 48 year old man with generalised anxiety disorder has had 12 weeks of high-intensity CBT. His symptoms remain severe and he is off work. He wants to try medication. He has no other illnesses.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate drug?
practice.e: Sertraline is the first-line drug for GAD. An SNRI such as venlafaxine is used if sertraline is ineffective or not tolerated.

steps.x: First drug for severe GAD.
Severe GAD despite therapy: start the first-line drug.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Sertraline** (SSRI).

elim: Tricyclics are not first-line for GAD.
Benzodiazepines cause dependence.
Propranolol only helps somatic symptoms.
Venlafaxine is second-line after an SSRI.

steps.x: **D. Sertraline.** Warn: 2 to 4 weeks to work, may worsen anxiety at first.

practice.stem: A 40 year old woman with generalised anxiety disorder has taken sertraline at an adequate dose for 10 weeks with little benefit and troublesome nausea. She is also having CBT. Her pulse rate is 86 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
practice.e: If sertraline is ineffective or not tolerated, offer another SSRI or an SNRI (venlafaxine, duloxetine). Benzodiazepines are avoided long-term.

steps.x: Next step when the first SSRI fails.

clues: sertraline at an adequate dose for 10 weeks
steps.x: Ineffective and poorly tolerated SSRI.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Switch to **another SSRI or an SNRI** such as **venlafaxine**.

elim: Long-term benzodiazepines cause dependence.
She is not tolerating it; propranolol only treats somatic symptoms.
She still has significant GAD.
Diazepam is a benzodiazepine: avoid long-term.

steps.x: **E. Switch to venlafaxine.**

practice.stem: A 25 year old woman with generalised anxiety disorder started sertraline 5 days ago. She says she feels more jittery and anxious than before. She asks why the tablets are making her worse.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Increased synaptic serotonin before limbic changes adapt
practice.e: SSRIs raise synaptic serotonin quickly but downregulate limbic hyperactivity only over weeks, explaining both the delayed benefit and early worsening.

steps.x: Mechanism: why do SSRIs make anxiety worse at first?

clues: more jittery and anxious than before
steps.x: Early paradoxical worsening on an SSRI.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Synaptic **serotonin rises quickly**; downregulation of limbic hyperactivity takes weeks.

elim: GABA-A downregulation explains benzodiazepine dependence.
SSRIs do not inhibit noradrenaline synthesis.
SSRIs increase, not deplete, synaptic serotonin.
Sertraline does not suppress the thyroid.

steps.x: **B. Increased synaptic serotonin before limbic changes adapt.**

Step 2 of stepped care.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: timing of review depends on age.

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the neurotransmitters and the acid-base change.

points.p: Hyperventilation causes respiratory alkalosis, lowering ionised calcium

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: link each drug to its mechanism.

glossary.GAD: Generalised anxiety disorder: excessive, uncontrollable worry about many things for at least 6 months.
glossary.generalised anxiety disorder: Chronic excessive worry about many everyday areas causing distress or impairment, lasting at least 6 months.
glossary.panic disorder: Recurrent sudden attacks of intense fear with breathlessness and palpitations.
glossary.panic attack: A sudden surge of intense fear peaking within minutes, with physical symptoms such as palpitations.
glossary.circumstantiality: Speech that takes long detours with unnecessary detail before reaching the point.
glossary.mental state exam: Structured assessment of appearance, behaviour, speech, mood, thought, perception and cognition.
glossary.affect: The outward expression of emotion seen by the examiner.
glossary.somatic: Relating to the body: physical symptoms such as palpitations or tremor.
glossary.hyperthyroidism: Overactive thyroid causing tremor, sweating, weight loss and palpitations; the key GAD mimic.
glossary.TFTs: Thyroid function tests: TSH and free T4.
glossary.TSH: Thyroid stimulating hormone; low in hyperthyroidism.
glossary.Holter monitor: Portable ECG recording over 24 or 48 hours to catch intermittent arrhythmias.
glossary.near-syncope: Feeling about to faint without losing consciousness.
glossary.syncope: Brief loss of consciousness from reduced blood flow to the brain.
glossary.CBT: Cognitive behavioural therapy: a talking therapy that changes unhelpful thoughts and behaviours.
glossary.psychoeducation: Teaching patients about their condition and how to manage it.
glossary.low-intensity psychological intervention: Brief therapy such as guided self-help or psychoeducation groups.
glossary.high-intensity psychological therapy: Individual therapy with a trained therapist, usually 12 to 15 sessions of CBT.
glossary.stepped care: Starting with the least intensive effective treatment and stepping up if it fails.
glossary.SSRI: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, such as sertraline.
glossary.sertraline: SSRI antidepressant; first-line drug for GAD.
glossary.SNRI: Serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor, such as venlafaxine or duloxetine.
glossary.venlafaxine: SNRI used if an SSRI fails or is not tolerated in GAD.
glossary.duloxetine: SNRI antidepressant, an alternative second-line drug in GAD.
glossary.beta-blockers: Drugs such as propranolol that block adrenaline's effect on the heart and muscles.
glossary.propranolol: Non-selective beta-blocker used to reduce palpitations and tremor in anxiety.
glossary.benzodiazepines: Sedative drugs such as diazepam that enhance GABA; avoided long-term because of dependence.
glossary.GABA-A receptor: Chloride channel receptor enhanced by benzodiazepines; downregulates with long-term use.
glossary.serotonin: Neurotransmitter (5-HT) involved in mood and anxiety; raised by SSRIs.
glossary.noradrenaline: Neurotransmitter driving the sympathetic fight-or-flight response.
glossary.amygdala: Brain region that detects threat and drives fear responses.
glossary.prefrontal cortex: Front part of the brain that regulates emotion and worry.
glossary.sympathetic: The fight-or-flight part of the autonomic nervous system.
glossary.respiratory alkalosis: Raised blood pH from blowing off too much CO2 by overbreathing.
glossary.hyperventilation: Breathing faster or deeper than the body needs, lowering CO2.
glossary.ionised calcium: The free, active fraction of blood calcium; falls in alkalosis.
glossary.dependence: Needing a drug to function normally, with withdrawal symptoms on stopping.
glossary.tolerance: Needing a higher dose for the same effect.
glossary.rebound anxiety: Anxiety worse than before, appearing when a drug is stopped.
glossary.GAD-7: Seven-question score of anxiety severity; 15 or more is severe.
glossary.NICE CG113: NICE guideline on generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder in adults.
